records.title: RapiDoc Portal documentation
records.subtitle: How to build a developer portal from OpenAPI specs and Markdown guides with RapiDoc Portal - configuration, guides, API reference pages, single sign-on (SSO), tools and deployment.
records.content: RapiDoc Portal turns your OpenAPI files and Markdown or Markdoc guides into a static developer portal, with search, an API catalog, interactive references and optional single sign-on. This site is built with it. What it offers at a glance is on RapiDoc Portal's page. The starter is a portal with an example API, a rapidoc.config.yaml and two guides, on http://localhost:4321. Already have a repository with OpenAPI files? Run npx @rapidoc/cli init there instead. Read the quickstart. In sync with RapiDoc 15, end to end: the same names, one sidebar and safer defaults across the family. From here on

records.title: Find your way
records.subtitle: RapiDoc Portal documentation
records.content: What a portal is made of, the quickstart, and the files of a project. rapidoc.config.yaml: the site, theme, header, navigation, APIs, workflows, footer and search. Markdown, Markdoc and MDX pages, callouts, live API operations and your own pages. Reference pages, API versions, the catalog, and RapiDoc's attributes. Sign-in with Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google or any OpenID Connect provider, and who may read what. A mock for every API, MCP for agents, spec checks, migrating, and hosting the port

records.title: Access rules
records.subtitle: Decide who may read which pages, APIs and files - by sign-in, group or email.
records.content: The access key of rapidoc.config.yaml decides who may read which pages, API references, specs and files. It works together with auth and is enforced by rapidoc serve; rapidoc dev shows everything. | Key | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | default | Who may read what no rule matches: any allow value below. Default public. | | rules | A list of { path, allow }, checked top to bottom. | | rules[].path | A URL path pattern, see below. | | rules[].allow | Who may read what the path matches, see Who may read. | :::caution[A rule must match something] A rule whose path matches no page or file fails the bui

records.title: Rules
records.subtitle: Access rules
records.content: Rules are checked top to bottom, and the first rule whose path matches decides . Put specific rules before general ones. path is a URL path on the site, starting with /: - matches one path segment: /docs/ /setup matches /docs/orders/setup. - matches any number of segments, including none: /docs/internal/ matches /docs/internal and everything under it. Guides in docs/internal/ are at /docs/internal/..., so the folder and the path match (Project structure).

records.title: Who may read: allow
records.subtitle: Access rules
records.content: | allow | Who may read | | :--- | :--- | | public | Everyone, signed in or not. | | signed-in | Anyone who has signed in: everyone your provider lets sign in, which may be more than your staff (who counts as signed in). | | { groups: [a, b] } | Signed-in readers in at least one of these groups. | | { emails: [' @acme.com', 'jo@partner.io'] } | Signed-in readers whose verified email matches one of these. matches any characters. | groups and emails can be combined in one allow: matching either one

records.subtitle: Access rules
records.content: An API's reference page, its tag pages, its spec file and its embedded operations are all under /apis/<id>, where <id> is the API's id under apis: (APIs). One rule covers all of them: This covers every version of the API too. To treat one version differently, put a rule for its URLs before the API's rule, since the first match decides:

records.title: What is protected
records.subtitle: Access rules
records.content: - Pages, specs, and the files of your project's public/ folder. - Search results: the search indexes are split per rule, so readers only find what they may read. - The sitemap lists only public pages. Not protected: the titles and paths of protected pages. Locked links stay visible in menus and the catalog with a lock icon, so readers know there is more behind sign-in; don't put anything confidential in a title or a URL. Always public: the site's scripts, styles and fonts, the RapiDoc bundle, th

records.subtitle: Access rules
records.content: | Request | Allowed | Signed out | Signed in, not allowed | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Page | 200 | Sent to your provider's sign-in, then back to the page | 403 "access denied" page | | Spec or other file | 200 | 401 | 403 |

records.title: Build warnings
records.subtitle: Access rules
records.content: - A protected API whose spec is a URL: the build warns, because the spec stays public at that URL. Protect it where it is hosted. - A public page that embeds an operation of a protected API: the build warns, because the operation won't load for readers who may not see the API.

records.subtitle: Step by step - put the portal behind Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) single sign-on, and give groups of employees access to their APIs with app roles.
records.content: This guide puts a portal behind your company's Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) sign-in: everyone in the company can read the portal, and only the billing team can read the billing API. Other providers work the same way; their differences are in Identity providers. It follows the same steps as Set up sign-in, with every Entra ID screen. Before you begin, you need: - a portal that builds (npx rapidoc build), - the address it will have, here https://developers.acme.com, - the right to register applications in your Entra tenant. 1. Register the portal in Entra ID In the Microsoft Entra admi

records.subtitle: SSO with Microsoft Entra ID

records.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
records.subtitle: Put the portal behind your company's single sign-on (SSO) with OpenID Connect (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Keycloak, Auth0), and decide who may read which pages and APIs.
records.content: When some guides or APIs are only for partners, customers or your own staff, readers can sign in with your company's single sign-on (SSO): Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Keycloak, Auth0, AWS Cognito, Ping, Authentik, Zitadel or any other OpenID Connect provider. SAML-only providers work through a broker (Identity providers). This page explains the parts and how to choose. To set it up, follow Set up sign-in, or SSO with Microsoft Entra ID for every Entra ID screen. Add two keys to rapidoc.config.yaml: - auth: readers sign in through your OpenID Connect provider. - access: rules th

records.title: Choose your setup
records.subtitle: Single sign-on (SSO)
records.content: | You need | Setup | | :--- | :--- | | Some pages or APIs public, others only for some readers or groups | auth and access, served by rapidoc serve. | | The whole portal private, every signed-in reader sees everything, with a sign-in button, per-reader search, and Try or agents using the reader's token | auth with access.default: signed-in, served by rapidoc serve. | | The whole portal private, nothing more | A plain static build behind your SSO proxy, with no portal server (Static hosting). | |

records.title: How it works
records.subtitle: Single sign-on (SSO)
records.content: A static site can show a sign-in button and hide links in the browser, but its files are still there for anyone who asks: pages, OpenAPI specs, attachments and the search index can be downloaded with their URL. So a portal with auth is served by rapidoc serve, which checks the reader before it sends anything protected: 1. rapidoc build sorts the output by the rules: dist/public/ (no protected content), dist/protected/, and dist/rapidoc-server.json with the rules. 2. rapidoc serve dist serves all

Default openid, profile, email. | | claims.groups | The claim with the reader's groups or roles, in the ID token or the provider's user info: a list, or names separated by spaces or commas. Default groups. Dotted paths work: realm access.roles. | | session.maxAge |

records.title: Identity providers
records.subtitle: The issuer URL, groups and Try audience for Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Google, AWS Cognito, Ping, Authentik and Zitadel, and SAML-only providers.
records.content: Single sign-on works with any OpenID Connect provider. This page has what differs between them; the steps are the same everywhere (Set up sign-in). For every Entra ID screen, see SSO with Microsoft Entra ID. At every provider, register a web application with the authorization code flow, its redirect URL <portal URL>/ rapidoc/auth/callback, and with logout: idp the portal URL as a post-logout redirect. A confidential client (with a client secret) and a public client (PKCE only) both work; set RAPIDOC AUTH CLIENT SECRET only for a confidential client. Issuer auth.issuer is the provider's sign-in

records.title: Issuer
records.subtitle: Identity providers
records.content: auth.issuer is the provider's sign-in service. Copy it exactly: with or without the trailing slash, as the provider shows it. | Provider | issuer | | :--- | :--- | | Okta | https://<org>.okta.com/oauth2/default (or another authorization server's URL) | | Microsoft Entra ID | https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant ID>/v2.0 | | Auth0 | https://<tenant>.<region>.auth0.com/, with the slash | | Keycloak | https://<host>/realms/<realm> | | Google | https://accounts.google.com | | AWS Cognito | http

records.title: Groups
records.subtitle: Identity providers
records.content: Access rules by group read the claim named in auth.claims.groups (default groups) from the ID token or the provider's user info. It must be a list of names, or names separated by spaces or commas. A dot in auth.claims.groups means a nested field (realm access.roles), so a claim name can't contain one. | Provider | Setting | | :--- | :--- | | Okta | On the authorization server, add a claim named groups to the ID token: Security → API → Authorization Servers → default → Claims → Add Claim , value

records.title: Audience for Try
records.subtitle: Identity providers
records.content: With tryIt, Try sends the reader's access token to your API, so the token has to be for your API: | Provider | Setting | | :--- | :--- | | Okta | Use your API's authorization server as issuer. Its tokens are for that server's audience. | | Microsoft Entra ID | Add your API's scope to scopes, for example api://<API's application ID>/access as user. | | Auth0 | Set audience to the API's identifier. | | Keycloak | Add an Audience mapper for your API's client to the portal's client. | | Google | Not

records.title: Google Workspace
records.subtitle: Identity providers
records.content: Google's ID token has no groups, so rules can use signed-in or emails; Google marks addresses as verified. To keep other Google accounts out, set the OAuth consent screen's User type to Internal : then only accounts of your Workspace organization can sign in.

records.title: SAML-only providers
records.subtitle: Identity providers
records.content: Put an OpenID Connect broker in front: Keycloak, Authentik, Zitadel or Ory Polis. The portal signs in with the broker, which signs in with your SAML provider. Each broker's documentation has the steps.

records.title: Try with the reader's token
records.subtitle: Let Try call your API with the signed-in reader's access token.
records.content: Every operation on an API reference page has a Try button, which sends the request to your API from the reader's browser. Without tryIt, readers fill in the Authentication panel of the reference page themselves: an API key, a token, or their own OAuth sign-in. With auth.tryIt, a signed-in reader presses Try and the request carries their own access token, from their sign-in to the portal. Your API's own permission check answers, with that reader's permissions: 200 for a reader who may call it, 403 for one who may not. There is no token to copy and paste. tryIt is optional. It needs: - portal si

records.title: How it works
records.subtitle: Try with the reader's token
records.content: 1. At sign-in, rapidoc serve keeps the reader's access token in its own encrypted, HttpOnly cookie. The ID and refresh tokens are not kept at all. 2. Reference pages and embedded operations ask the server for the token, and fill it into the authentication panel for one security scheme of the spec: - the first oauth2 or openIdConnect scheme, - else the first HTTP bearer scheme. 3. Try sends Authorization: Bearer <token> to the API. The page keeps the token in memory only, never in local storage.

records.title: The audience
records.subtitle: Try with the reader's token
records.content: The access token has to be for your API, not for the portal. Okta: use your API's authorization server as issuer. Auth0: set audience to the API's identifier. Microsoft Entra ID: add your API's scope to scopes, such as api://<API's application ID>/access as user. Every provider: Audience for Try.

records.title: Before your API exists: the mock server
records.subtitle: Try with the reader's token
records.content: Point the spec's server at rapidoc mock, which checks each token's signature, audience and scopes the way your API would: Signed-in readers then get 200 or 403 from the mock, depending on their own scopes. Okta's default authorization server issues tokens for the audience api://default.

records.title: Linking to an operation
records.subtitle: Reference pages
records.content: Give every operation an operationId. The anchor is then stable: Without an operationId, the anchor is built from the summary and changes when the summary is edited, so rapidoc dev and rapidoc build warn about such operations. Every operation can also be linked by its method and path, which only changes with the endpoint: get-orders-orderid.

records.title: OAuth 2 sign-in for Try
records.subtitle: Reference pages
records.content: Readers can sign in to your API from the API reference page and call it with Try , using their own account. The sign-in runs in the browser, so it works on a plain static portal: no auth key and no rapidoc serve. It covers calls to your API only; the documentation stays public.

records.title: How it works
records.subtitle: Reference pages
records.content: 1. The spec declares an oauth2 or openIdConnect security scheme. RapiDoc shows it in the page's Authentication section. 2. The reader presses Authorize . RapiDoc opens your provider's sign-in in a popup, using the authorization code flow with PKCE. 3. The provider redirects the popup to /oauth-receiver.html, a page every portal build has. It hands the code back to the API page, and RapiDoc exchanges it for an access token at the tokenUrl. 4. Try sends Authorization: Bearer <token> to your API. T

records.title: Declare the scheme
records.subtitle: Reference pages
records.content: Use a standard OpenAPI oauth2 scheme. For a public client, pre-fill the client ID with x-client-id and set x-pkce-only: true, which hides the client secret fields, so readers only press Authorize : More extensions, such as x-authorize-params and x-token-params for an audience, are in RapiDoc's OAuth guide.

records.title: At your provider

records.title: Introduction
records.subtitle: What RapiDoc Portal is, what it builds, and which package does what.
records.content: RapiDoc Portal is a docs-as-code developer portal framework. You keep your OpenAPI specs and your guides in a repository, describe the site in one rapidoc.config.yaml, and the rapidoc command builds a static portal from them. A portal has: - A home page from docs/index.md, .mdx or .markdoc. - Guides under /docs/..., written in Markdown, MDX or Markdoc (Markdown with tags, made by Stripe). - An interactive API reference for each spec at /apis/<id>, rendered by the RapiDoc web component. Each operation has a Try button that sends a real request to your API from the browser. - An API catalog at /

records.title: Why another portal framework?
records.subtitle: Introduction
records.content: - Docs as code. Everything is a file in your repository: review it in pull requests, build it in CI. - Static by default. No database and no runtime to operate. Per-page sign-in is the one feature that needs a server, and it's opt-in. A portal that is private as a whole can sit behind your SSO proxy as static files (Static hosting). - Strict config. An unknown key fails the build with its path and a hint, so a typo never disappears silently. - Accessible. The layout is tested against WCAG 2.1 AA

records.subtitle: Mock server
records.content: Examples from the spec first, else data generated from the schema; requests are validated against the spec; Prefer headers pick a documented response (Prefer: code=404); CORS is allowed for any origin. records.title: Real token checks
records.subtitle: Mock server
records.content: Each operation's security is enforced. Start the mock with your OpenID Connect issuer, and bearer tokens must be signed by it, unexpired, for your audience and carry the operation's scopes (else 401 or 403): --issuer and --audience can also come from RAPIDOC MOCK ISSUER and RAPIDOC MOCK AUDIENCE. Without --issuer, any bearer token passes and scopes aren't checked. Combined with Try with the reader's token, signed-in readers see 200 or 403 depending on their own permissions.

records.title: Showing tag source in a code block
records.subtitle: Markdoc
records.content: A code fence shows its content as text, tags included, so the examples on this page are plain fences. Markdoc still checks the tags inside a fence, though: an unknown tag or attribute fails the build even inside a code block. To show tags that aren't valid here, such as a tag from another site or a made-up example, turn the check off with Markdoc's process=false annotation after the language: markdoc Shown as text, never checked. ` Code fences in markdoc are highlighted as Markdown.

records.subtitle: MDX
records.content: The components Aside, CardGrid, LinkCard, LinkButton, FileTree and Icon are exported from @rapidoc/portal/components. Import the ones you use: Icon draws a Phosphor icon at 24px; size={16} makes it smaller. The portal uses Phosphor icons only, so icons in guides match the header and sidebar.

records.title: A page inside the portal's frame
records.subtitle: Your own pages
records.content: PortalLayout gives a page the portal's header, footer, theme and head tags: The page can use the portal's other components (Card, Tabs, Icon, ...) and your own, like an MDX page.

records.title: A page with its own document
records.subtitle: Your own pages
records.content: A page that writes its own <html> gets none of the portal's styles, which is what a full-screen demo wants. PortalHead adds what every page of the site should still have: the title from site.titleTemplate, the description, the favicon, the link-preview tags and the head: entries of the config, such as analytics. Import PortalHead by that path, not from @rapidoc/portal/components: importing from there brings the portal's styles to the page.

records.title: With the portal's header
records.subtitle: Your own pages
records.content: A page with its own document can still have the portal's header, so the whole site has one: the same links, menus and search, from header in the config. The header brings the portal's colors and your theme.css with it, and nothing else: the rest of the page keeps the styles you give it. Set data-theme on <html> to dark or light, which is the theme the header draws in. A page with one theme only should hide the header's light/dark switcher in its own CSS (.portal-theme-btn). records.subtitle: Your own pages
records.content: Every portal has a 404 page: the header, a short message, and ways back (the home page, the search and the navigation tabs). To use your own, add pages/404.astro. It replaces the portal's, and can use PortalLayout or its own document like any other page. records.title: Search
records.subtitle: Your own pages
records.content: Your pages are in the portal's search, next to the guides and the API operations, under a Pages filter. A page is found by its <h1> (or its <title>), its description and its text, and each <h2> and <h3> that has an id is a result of its own that opens the page at that heading. The search reads your pages as HTML, since they have no Markdown source. Two things follow: - Only text in the page's HTML counts. records.subtitle: Your own pages
records.content: - llms.txt : your own pages are not listed there. - The sidebar : link to a page from header.links, the footer or a guide. - With a base path (site.url with a path): write links through the portal's components, or add the base yourself in plain <a> tags. With sign-in, access: rules apply to your pages by path, like every other page. rapidoc dev reloads a page when you edit it, and restarts when you add or remove one.
